title: Compost and Soil
description: Look closely at soil ingredients and the organic materials found in a garden’s compost area.
cardDescription: Look closely at soil ingredients and the organic materials found in a garden’s compost area.
focus: Particle sizes and organic matter describe different aspects of soil. The clues distinguish loam from a single mineral fraction and humus from both fresh leaves and the food with a similar name.
solvingTip: Sort the definitions into particle, mixture, process, or organic material. The shortest garden words help with the less familiar soil terms.
words: Dark relatively stable organic matter formed as material decomposes
Soil texture containing a mixture of sand, silt, and clay
Decomposed organic material made from collected plant and other suitable matter
Layer spread over the soil surface around plants
Soil particle size between sand and clay
Finest of the three main mineral soil particle groups
Coarsest of the three main mineral soil particle groups
Earthy growing medium beneath a garden's plants
Fallen tree part added to many garden compost piles
Burrowing animal often found in moist garden soil
Gas-filled space needed within a well-structured soil
Liquid occupying some of a soil's pore spaces
Heap of collected material in a compost area
To decay as organic material breaks down

answerNotes.HUMUS: Humus is soil organic matter. Its spelling differs from hummus, the chickpea-based food.
answerNotes.LOAM: Loam combines mineral particle sizes. It is not simply another name for compost or for any fertile soil.
answerNotes.COMPOST: Compost is a product of managed decomposition. Its ingredients and degree of breakdown affect its properties.
answerNotes.MULCH: Mulch covers the surface. Compost can be used as mulch, but the two words describe different things: a material and a use.
answerNotes.SILT: Silt particles are smaller than sand and larger than clay. These names describe mineral size fractions rather than organic ingredients.

title: A Trellis of Garden Peas
description: Follow climbing peas through their supports, curling structures, and seed-bearing pods.
cardDescription: Follow climbing peas through their supports, curling structures, and seed-bearing pods.
focus: Peas use tendrils to hold onto supports. This differs from plants that climb mainly by winding their stems, so the clues keep the plant and its climbing mechanism connected.
solvingTip: Distinguish the living climbing part from the support supplied by a gardener. A fruit, a seed, and a stem are also separate structures.
words: Slender curling plant structure a pea uses to grasp support
Framework provided for climbing garden plants
Seed-bearing fruit of a pea plant
Strong thin cord used for tying garden supports
Climbing or trailing plant stem, as in a pea planting
Tall upright support beside a climbing plant
Individual pea from which a new plant can grow
Plant axis bearing leaves and supporting growth
Flat green structure carrying out much of a pea plant's photosynthesis
To grow upward along a supporting framework
Plant structure anchoring the pea below ground
To fasten a support with a piece of cord
Small round seed inside this garden plant's pod
Pointed support pushed into garden soil

answerNotes.TENDRIL: A pea uses tendrils to hold nearby supports. Many climbing beans instead wind their stems, which is a different mechanism.
answerNotes.TRELLIS: A trellis is a support, not a living plant part. Its openings give tendrils or stems places to hold.
answerNotes.POD: A pea pod is a fruit in botanical terms. The individual peas inside are seeds.
answerNotes.TWINE: Twine is a supplied material. It differs from a tendril grown by the pea plant itself.
answerNotes.VINE: Vine describes a growth habit. Different vines attach or climb in different ways.

title: Bulbs and Other Underground Stores
description: Separate familiar underground plant structures through examples from flowers and the vegetable garden.
cardDescription: Separate familiar underground plant structures through examples from flowers and the vegetable garden.
focus: Bulbs, corms, tubers, and rhizomes are not interchangeable botanical terms. The clues identify their structures and use specific examples, including a true bulb and a solid corm.
solvingTip: Use the plant example with the structural definition. Layered, solid, swollen, and horizontal describe different storage forms.
words: Underground storage structure with fleshy leaf bases, as in an onion
Solid swollen underground stem, as in a crocus
Swollen storage structure exemplified by a potato stem
Horizontal stem often growing underground, as in bearded iris
Garden flower that stores food in tuberous roots
Bearded ___, flowering plant commonly grown from a rhizome
Spring flower growing from a true bulb
Early spring flower growing from a corm
Kitchen vegetable whose layered underground part is a bulb
Plant organ whose fleshy base forms part of a true bulb
Underground organ that absorbs water and anchors a plant
Function served by these food-holding plant structures
Undeveloped growing point from which a shoot may emerge

answerNotes.BULB: A bulb contains fleshy leaf bases around a short stem. An onion provides a familiar example of that layered structure.
answerNotes.CORM: A corm is solid stem tissue. It differs from the layered fleshy leaf bases of a true bulb.
answerNotes.TUBER: A potato is a stem tuber. Other plants, such as dahlias, have tuberous roots rather than the same stem structure.
answerNotes.RHIZOME: A rhizome is a stem, even when it lies below ground. Some irises have bulbs, so the clue specifically names bearded iris.
answerNotes.DAHLIA: Dahlia storage structures are tuberous roots. They should not be described as potato-like stem tubers.

title: At the Rose Arbor
description: Examine a rose plant and its garden framework through precise plant parts and familiar outdoor structures.
cardDescription: Examine a rose plant and its garden framework through precise plant parts and familiar outdoor structures.
focus: Roses have prickles rather than true botanical thorns. A climbing rose’s long canes are generally trained onto a support, while the arbor and lattice belong to the garden structure.
solvingTip: Decide whether each clue names the plant or its support. A flowering part, a fruit, and a protective projection have different names.
words: Sharp surface outgrowth on a rose stem
Long woody stem of a rose plant
Fruit that develops on a rose after flowering
Garden framework forming a sheltered passage or sitting place
Framework of crossed narrow strips used as a plant support
Flowering shrub featured on this garden framework
One colored segment surrounding a rose flower's center
Unopened flower on a rose cane
Plant axis supporting a rose's leaves and flowers
Fragrance noticed near a blooming rose
Open support against which long rose canes may be trained
Curved overhead shape of some garden entrances
Structure helping a long rose cane stay in position
Green plant part along a rose stem
Cord used to secure a stem to a garden framework

answerNotes.PRICKLE: A rose's sharp projections are botanically prickles. True thorns are modified branches, a different structure.
answerNotes.CANE: Rose growers call the longer stems canes. Climbing roses have long canes that can be trained onto supports rather than true twining vines.
answerNotes.HIP: A rose hip is the fruit. It is different from the unopened flower bud that appears before the bloom.
answerNotes.ARBOR: An arbor is a garden structure that can support plants. It is separate from the living rose growing over it.
answerNotes.LATTICE: Lattice has an open crisscross pattern. It can form part of an arbor or a trellis.

title: A Patch of Garden Berries
description: Explore berry plants through their growth habits, harvest words, and a few distinctive fruits.
cardDescription: Explore berry plants through their growth habits, harvest words, and a few distinctive fruits.
focus: The everyday word berry includes fruits with different botanical structures. These clues use common garden names while distinguishing a strawberry runner from a bramble’s woody cane.
solvingTip: A clue about spreading or new growth may name a plant structure. A fruit clue gives a familiar garden name rather than a strict botanical category.
words: Horizontal strawberry stem that can form new plantlets
Prickly shrub group including blackberries and raspberries
Fruit that usually leaves its central receptacle behind when picked
Small blue fruit growing on a woody shrub
Small clustered fruit also sold in red or black varieties
Red garden fruit whose plant commonly spreads by runners
Woody stem of a raspberry or blackberry plant
Dark bramble fruit retaining its central core when picked
Round shrub fruit whose plant often has spiny stems
Mature and ready to pick, as garden fruit
Seed-bearing plant structure harvested from a berry patch
To gather a crop when it is ready
To remove an individual ripe fruit from its plant
Straight line of plants in a garden patch
Open mesh used to cover some fruit plantings
Small developing shoot on a berry cane

answerNotes.RUNNER: A strawberry runner is a stem used in vegetative spread. New plantlets can take root at points along it.
answerNotes.BRAMBLE: Bramble is a familiar collective word for these plants. It is not a name for the fruit alone.
answerNotes.RASPBERRY: A picked raspberry is commonly hollow at the center. A blackberry generally retains the central receptacle within the picked fruit.
answerNotes.BLUEBERRY: Blueberries grow on shrubs rather than on strawberry-like runners. Common food names do not all reflect the same botanical fruit type.
answerNotes.CURRANT: Fresh currants grow on shrubs. They are distinct from the dried small grapes also marketed as Zante currants.
